1.q: Which statements about RAM and storage are true?
o: RAM is volatile.
Storage is non-volatile.
The CPU executes a program directly from storage.
More storage lets you run more programs at once.
A running process is lost at power-off while its program file remains.
1.e: Storage is the permanent copy and RAM is the working copy.
w: True: Its contents are lost when power is removed.
True: SSDs and HDDs keep data without power.
False: The program must be loaded into RAM first.
False: Running programs live in RAM, so RAM limits that.
True: The process was in RAM; the file is in storage.

1.q: A laptop has 1 TB of SSD but only 4 GB of RAM and feels slow with many windows open. Which explanations are justified?
o: The OS runs short of RAM and has to close or juggle programs.
The SSD is too fast.
A big disk does not give more room for running programs.
Adding more RAM would help more than adding more storage.
The GPU has no cores.
1.e: Memory is not storage: capacity of one does not substitute for the other.
w: True: Too little RAM is the limit when many programs run.
False: Speed of storage is not the cause of this slowness.
True: Running programs occupy RAM, not storage.
True: RAM is the resource being exhausted.
False: This does not follow from the symptom.

1.q: Which statements about the CPU are correct?
o: It fetches, decodes and executes instructions.
A higher GHz means more cycles per second.
More cores always make every program four times faster.
More cores can improve multitasking but use more power.
The clock coordinates actions in the computer.
1.e: Cores and clock speed are different properties with different trade-offs.
w: True: That is its basic cycle.
True: GHz measures the clock rate.
False: Cores help parallel work and cost power; not every task speeds up.
True: This is the trade-off of multi-core designs.
True: It is a series of pulses that keeps the parts in step.

o: RAM
Cache
SSD
HDD
A file saved on the SSD
1.e: Only RAM and cache are volatile in this list.
w: True: It loses contents without power.
True: It is fast volatile memory.

1.q: Using the course rule for prefixes, which are correct?
o: 1 GB = 10⁹ B.
1 TB = 2⁴⁰ B.
20 GB holds about 5 × 10⁹ four-byte emoji.
1 MB = 10⁶ B.
1.e: Powers of ten, not powers of two.
w: False: The course ignores binary prefixes; 1 TB is 10¹² B.

1.q: Which statements describe what happens when you open a browser?
o: The program is loaded from storage into RAM.
RAM supplies instructions and data to the CPU.
The GPU can handle graphics such as video and animation.
The CPU copies the program back to cache permanently.
Results can be saved back to storage.
1.e: Storage → RAM → CPU → results, with the GPU handling graphics.
w: True: Storage holds the file; RAM holds the running process.
True: The CPU works from RAM.
False: Cache is volatile and holds only frequently used data.
True: That is how work persists.

1.q: Which statements about a laptop specification are correct?
o: "1920 × 1080" is the resolution in pixels, width by height.
"15-inch" is the diagonal length of the display.
"12 MB cache" is fast volatile memory inside the CPU.
"1 TB SSD" is volatile memory.
"Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5" describe wireless connectivity.
1.e: Each spec line names one component and its measure.
w: False: An SSD is non-volatile storage.
True: Wi-Fi is long range; Bluetooth is short range.

1.q: Which statements about embedded systems are true?
o: They are computers dedicated to a narrow range of functions.
They can be found in microwaves, cars and watches.
They have no processor or memory.
They are part of a larger system.
The BBC micro:bit has sensors.
1.e: Same three resources, in a small dedicated package.
w: False: Even a micro:bit has a processor, memory and storage.
True: That is how they differ from a general-purpose computer.
True: It is a tiny embedded computer with sensors.

1.q: A student claims "Software is stored in RAM, so RAM is the same as storage." Which responses are correct?
o: Programs are stored in storage and copied to RAM to run.
RAM is volatile; storage is not.
The CPU cannot run a program straight from storage.
RAM is slower than storage.
Both lose data at power-off.
1.e: The two are different layers with different roles.
w: True: Storage is the permanent location.
True: That is the central difference.
True: It must be loaded into RAM.
False: RAM is faster than storage.
False: Storage keeps data without power.

1.q: Which statements are correct about the GPU and display?
o: The GPU is a processor for graphics.
It relieves the CPU of graphics work.
GPUs are used for parallel matrix computation such as machine learning.
A GPU measures screen size.
HDMI sends digital audio and video to a monitor or TV.
1.e: The GPU handles graphics and parallel numeric work.
w: True: It handles games, video and animation.
False: Screen size is the display diagonal.

2.q: Which are roles of an operating system?
o: Manage resources such as memory and storage.
Provide an interface for a human to interact with the computer.
Allow application programs to use those resources.
Manufacture the CPU.
Share resources among programs that want them.
2.e: All roles revolve around sharing resources nicely.
w: True: This is a core role.
True: Applications reach hardware through the OS.
False: Hardware is built by manufacturers, not by the OS.

2.q: Which statements about programs and processes are true?
o: A program is an executable file stored in non-volatile storage.
A process is a program in execution.
A process lives in storage.
When power is cut, the process terminates but the program remains.
Task Manager (Windows) or Activity Monitor (macOS) shows processes.
w: True: It is the running instance.
False: A process lives in RAM.
True: RAM is volatile; storage is not.
True: These are the tools for viewing them.

2.q: A user presses Ctrl-z while top is running, then types fg and presses Ctrl-c. Which statements are correct?
o: Ctrl-z suspended top and moved it out of the foreground.
fg brought top back to the foreground.
Ctrl-c terminated top.
Ctrl-z killed top and freed all its RAM.
While suspended, top used no CPU.
2.e: Pause is not kill: a suspended process keeps its RAM.
w: True: fg resumes in the foreground.
True: It kills the foreground process.
False: Suspended processes still hold their RAM.
True: A suspended process is not running.

2.q: Which statements about killing and suspending a process are true?
o: Killing frees both CPU and RAM.
Suspending frees the CPU.
Suspending frees the RAM.
bg resumes a suspended process in the background.
A suspended process is gone for good.
w: False: A suspended process still holds its RAM.
True: This is the purpose of bg.
False: It can be resumed with fg or bg.

2.q: Which statements about the CLI are correct?
o: It is also called the terminal, shell or command line.
Linux commands are almost always lowercase.
Options typically come before arguments.
The order of options matters a great deal.
Tab completion and the arrow keys save typing.
w: True: Those names are used interchangeably.
True: They complete names and recall history.

2.q: Which are valid reasons the course uses Linux?
o: It powers over 60% of servers worldwide.
It runs all of the Top 500 supercomputers.
Android is built on the Linux kernel.
It cannot be used from the command line.
It prepares students for advanced IS courses.
2.e: Linux is everywhere in servers and infrastructure.
w: False: It is the CLI that makes Linux useful for administration.
True: Stated as the course goal.

2.q: Which are duties of the OS in "sharing nicely"?
o: Processor scheduling.
Memory allocation.
Storage and I/O coordination.
Designing the application interface of every program.
Providing user interfaces such as the GUI and CLI.
2.e: Four duties: scheduling, memory, storage and I/O, interfaces.
w: True: Programs take turns on the CPU.
True: Isolated RAM space per process.
True: File requests become block reads and writes.
False: Each application designs its own interface.

2.q: Which statements about booting are correct?
o: Firmware loads the OS kernel from non-volatile storage into memory.
The OS then takes control of the computer.
The OS must be loaded from RAM at power-up.
Storage must hold the OS for it to start.
Booting happens each time power is applied.
2.e: The OS lives in storage and is loaded into memory at boot.
w: True: That is the boot step.
False: RAM is empty at power-up.
True: It is loaded from storage.
True: RAM is volatile, so it is repeated.

2.q: Which are correct about foreground and background processes?
o: The foreground process is the one you are interacting with.
Background processes run without direct user interaction.
Ctrl-c terminates the background process.
A GUI analogy: minimised apps are background.
Only one process can exist at a time.
2.e: Foreground is the one in focus.
w: False: It terminates the foreground process.
False: Many processes exist at once; one is in the foreground.

2.q: Which statements about software categories are correct?
o: A terminal is application software.
Windows, Linux and macOS are system software.
The OS is the core component of system software.
A web browser is system software.
Application software solves specific user needs.
2.e: Applications serve users; system software serves the machine.

3.q: Using yum.csv (20 data rows plus a header), which commands correctly count the unique foods?
o: tail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d"," -f2 | sort | uniq | wc -l
cut -d"," -f2 yum.csv | uniq | wc -l
tail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d"," -f2 | uniq | wc -l
tail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d"," -f2 | sort -u | wc -l
grep -c food yum.csv
3.e: The unique count needs sorted input for uniq, or sort -u.
w: True: Skip header, take food, sort, collapse, count: 16.
False: Without sort, non-adjacent repeats stay.
False: Without sort, repeated foods that are not adjacent are counted twice.
True: sort -u removes duplicates; the result is 16.
False: That counts lines containing the word food.

3.q: Which statements about the pipeline tail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d"," -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -n -r | head -n 1 are correct?
o: It skips the header row.
It prints the most common food with its count.
The first line printed is "3 Sushi".
sort -n -r sorts the counts in ascending order.
uniq -c counts the occurrences of adjacent identical lines.
3.e: Top-N is a sort, count, sort, head pattern.
w: True: The first line after a numeric reverse sort.
True: Sushi appears three times, the most.
True: After sorting, that is every occurrence.

3.q: Which commands give the number of lines that contain "Sushi" in yum.csv?
o: grep "Sushi" yum.csv | wc -l
grep -c Sushi yum.csv | wc
cat yum.csv | grep "Sushi" | wc -l
wc -l Sushi
grep "Sushi" yum.csv
3.e: grep selects lines and wc -l counts them.
w: False: wc here is not the right count.
True: Same result with cat first.
False: wc counts lines in a file called Sushi.
False: That prints the lines; it does not count them.

3.q: Which statements about sort are correct?
o: By default it sorts alphabetically.
Without -n, "10" sorts before "9".
-n sorts numerically.
-r reverses the order.
sort changes the original file.
3.e: Use -n whenever the column is numeric.
w: False: It writes to the output only.

3.q: A student runs cat yum.csv | cut -d"," -f3 | sort | head -n 1 to find the lowest price. Which statements are correct?
o: The header word "price" is part of the data being sorted.
The command prints 3, the lowest price.
The command prints 10, because sort compares text and "10" comes before "3".
Adding tail -n +2 and sort -n fixes both problems and prints 3.
The header sorts first because # comes before the digits.
3.e: Skip the header and sort numerically.
w: True: Nothing removes the header row.
False: Text order puts "10" ahead of "3".
True: Characters are compared left to right.
True: Skip the header and compare numerically.
False: The third column of the header is "price", which sorts after the digits.

o: > creates the file or overwrites it.
>> appends to the end of the file.
> file.txt on its own empties the file but keeps it.
>> deletes the previous contents first.
echo "a" >> f twice leaves two lines.
3.e: One arrow overwrites, two arrows append.

3.q: Which commands accept more than one file argument directly?
o: cat f1 f2
head f1 f2
wc *.log
cut f1 f2
grep "error" *.log
3.e: cut and uniq take a single input; pipe cat into them.
w: False: Use cat files | cut instead.

o: ls *.csv lists all files ending in .csv.
ls s?m? matches four-letter names with s first and m third.
? matches zero or more characters.
* matches exactly one character.
ls so* lists names starting with so.
3.e: Star is many, question mark is one.
w: True: ? is exactly one character each.

3.q: Which statements about uniq options are correct?
o: -c prefixes each line with its count.
-d shows only lines that are duplicated.
-u shows only lines that appear once.
-n sorts the lines.
All of them work on adjacent lines, so sort first.
w: False: uniq has no sorting option.

3.q: In Lab 1, which commands correctly list the foods that cost exactly 5, in alphabetical order?
o: tail -n +2 yum.csv | grep ",5," | cut -d"," -f2 | sort
grep "5" yum.csv | sort
cut -d"," -f3 yum.csv | grep 5
tail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d"," -f2 | grep 5
sort yum.csv | head -n 5
3.e: Match the surrounding commas so that 15 and 50 are not matched.
w: True: ",5," matches only the price column.
False: It also matches 15 and the date digits.
False: That prints prices, not foods.
False: The food column does not contain prices.
False: That prints the first five lines.

4.q: Which statements about absolute and relative paths are true?
o: An absolute path begins at the root and starts with /.
A relative path starts from the current working directory.
A relative path may start with /.
.. refers to the parent directory.
pwd prints your current absolute path.
w: True: It is unique and unambiguous.
True: It is interpreted from where you are.
False: A leading / makes a path absolute.

4.q: The CWD is /home/jones. Which resolutions are correct?
o: donations → /home/jones/donations
../smith/reports → /home/smith/reports
../../dev/ttyE71 → /dev/ttyE71
utilities/printall → /utilities/printall
. → /home/jones
4.e: Apply each .. one level at a time.
w: True: A plain name is below the CWD.
True: One level up, then down.
True: Two levels up reaches the root.
False: It is relative to the CWD, not the root.

4.q: Which statements about permissions on a directory are correct?
o: r lets you list its contents.
x lets you enter it with cd.
w lets you create, delete or rename items inside.
x lets you edit the files inside.
Without x, cd fails even if you can read the directory.
4.e: Directory x is about entering, not editing.
w: False: File contents depend on file permissions.

4.q: Which chmod commands make notes.txt readable and writable by the owner only?
o: chmod u=rw,go= notes.txt
chmod u+rw notes.txt
chmod u=rw, go= notes.txt
chmod go-rwx notes.txt, if the owner already has rw
chmod a+rw notes.txt
4.e: Symbolic chmod has no spaces; go- removes group and world rights.
w: False: It adds rw for the owner but does not remove any group or world access.
True: It removes all access from group and world.
False: That gives everybody read and write.

4.q: After cp * ../../bravo/banana/ is run in alpha/mango (fomo.txt, savage.txt), which statements are correct?
o: The two files are copied into banana.
mango still contains both files.
mango is now empty.
rm ../../bravo/banana/fomo.txt removes only the copy.
The original names in mango changed.
4.e: cp does not remove the original.
w: True: It names the copy in banana.

4.q: Which statements about file types are correct?
o: Renaming virus.exe to funny-cat.jpg does not change what the file is.
A .docx is a binary file.
Text files are not stored as binary digits.
The extension helps the OS choose a program to open the file.
A file can be converted by changing its extension.
w: True: The content stays the same.
True: It embeds formatting, fonts and media.
False: All files are binary digits; text is how they are interpreted.

4.q: Which statements about PATH are correct?
o: It is a list of directories searched for executables.
The OS searches them in order and runs the first match.
It lists every file on the computer.
If printall is in a PATH directory you can run it by name.
It is only used on Windows.
w: True: No full path is needed.

4.q: Which of these are correct about hidden files and ls?
o: A name starting with . is hidden.
ls shows hidden files by default.
ls -a shows hidden files.
After mkdir one .two three, plain ls shows one and three.
ls -l hides the permissions.

4.q: Why must execute permission be granted explicitly?
o: So that you do not run a malicious downloaded file by accident.
A downloaded script gives Permission denied until chmod u+x.
Because Linux cannot run scripts.
chmod +x gives execute to all categories.
It is only needed for directories.
w: True: The default has no x.
False: It can, once x is set.
False: Files need it to run as programs.

4.q: Which statements about moving around the tree are correct?
o: cd with no arguments goes to the home directory.
cd - returns to the previous directory.
cd . changes to the parent.
tree shows a visual tree from the current folder.
cd .. goes up one level.
4.e: Dot is here, dot-dot is up.

5.q: Which statements about packet switching are correct?
o: Messages are split into numbered packets.
Packets may take different routes.
Packets always arrive in order.
The receiver reassembles the packets.
Routers know the full path from sender to receiver.
5.e: Independent routes, reassembly at the end.
w: True: This lets them be reassembled.
False: They can arrive out of order.
False: They know only the next hop.

5.q: Which four items does each packet carry?
o: Destination IP address.
Destination port number.
Source IP address.
Source port number.
The user name of the sender.
5.e: IPs identify computers; ports identify processes.
w: True: So the reply reaches the right process.
False: Not part of a packet header.

5.q: Which statements about IP addresses are correct?
o: IPv4 has 32 bits, about 4.3 billion addresses.
IPv6 has 128 bits.
IPv6 works in parallel with IPv4.
127.0.0.1 leaves the device through the router.
A hostname is the human-readable form of an address.
w: False: Loopback stays inside the device.
True: DNS maps it to an IP.

5.q: Which statements about port numbers are correct?
o: A port identifies the process that should receive the data.
Two processes on the same computer cannot share a port.
To run two web servers on one computer, give them different ports.
HTTP defaults to 443.
SSH defaults to 22.
5.e: Ports are the second half of the address.

5.q: Which statements about DNS are correct?
o: It translates hostnames to IP addresses.
The browser first asks the default DNS server, often on the router.
Without DNS we would need to memorise IP addresses.
In node7.cluster.spider.net, the TLD is node7.
DNS is a distributed system.
w: True: Then the chain continues if unknown.
True: A key reason it exists.

5.q: Which statements about ping are correct?
o: A reply shows the host is reachable and gives round-trip time.
A timeout proves the host is down.
A name-resolution failure points to a DNS problem.
ping tells you whether a port is open.
Ping failure is inconclusive.
5.e: No reply does not prove the host is down.
w: False: It could also be a firewall blocking ICMP.
True: The name could not be turned into an IP.

5.q: A website will not load. Which diagnosis steps are in a sensible order?
o: ping 1.1.1.1 to test local connectivity.
dig +short example.com to test DNS.
nmap example.com -p 443 to check the port.
nmap first, then replace the router.
filtered suggests a firewall or security group is blocking.
w: True: A name that does not resolve is a DNS problem.
True: The server may still be running.

5.q: Which statements distinguish closed from filtered?
o: Closed: the host answers and no application listens on that port.
Filtered: a firewall blocks the probe, so the state is unknown.
Closed and filtered mean the same.
Open: an application is listening.
Filtered always means the server is down.
w: False: The server may be running.

5.q: Which statements about types of networks are correct?
o: A LAN covers a small area such as a home or office.
A WAN connects LANs over a large distance.
The Internet is a WAN that spans the planet.
A gateway handles communication between a LAN and other networks.
Wireless networks are immune to interference.
w: False: They are prone to interference and security issues.

5.q: A client in a client-server exchange ...
o: initiates a request.
receives a response from a server.
is always listening for incoming requests.
can be a browser.
must be on the same LAN as the server.
w: True: That is how the exchange completes.
False: Servers can be anywhere reachable.

6.q: Which statements about the Internet and the World Wide Web are correct?
o: The Internet is the physical network infrastructure.
The Web is an application system on top of the Internet.
A search engine is a website that helps find other websites.
A browser is a web server.
A website is a collection of related web pages.
6.e: Web pages, sites, browsers and servers are Web concepts.
w: False: A browser is the client.
True: From the same person or organisation.

6.q: Which statements about HTML and CSS are correct?
o: HTML defines structure and content.
CSS controls how content looks.
The browser honours every extra blank line you type in HTML.
Tags are written in angle brackets.
Improperly nested tags can give unpredictable rendering.
6.e: Content and look are separate concerns.
w: False: It ignores extra spaces and line breaks.

6.q: A page references 3 images, 1 stylesheet and 1 script. Which statements are correct?
o: The browser first receives the base HTML.
The page needs 6 HTTP requests in total.
Only 1 request is needed because the HTML includes the images.
Each secondary file gets its own request.
A missing image file returns an HTTP error such as 404.
6.e: n + 1 generalises to every referenced object.
w: True: It parses it and finds the other files.

6.q: Which statements about HTTP are correct?
o: It is a request and response protocol between client and server.
A browser or httpie can be the HTTP client.
HTTP encrypts traffic by default.
HTTPS gives confidentiality and integrity.
The server waits for requests and sends back resources.
6.e: Plain HTTP is readable on the wire.
w: True: The browser asks; the server answers.
True: Any program that sends requests.

6.q: For http://localhost:8000/animals/cat/../.. with web root public_html, which statements are correct?
o: .. goes up one directory.
The URL resolves to public_html itself.
It serves index.html if that file exists.
It gives a 404 because .. is not allowed.
If there is no index.html, a directory listing is shown.
6.e: URL paths work like file paths.
w: True: As in a file system.
True: Two levels up from animals/cat.
True: A directory request gets index.html.
False: The path resolves to the web root.

6.q: Which statements about the parts of a URL are correct?
o: The scheme says how the resource is accessed, such as http or https.
The host tells the client which server to contact.
If the port is omitted, http uses 80 and https uses 443.
The anchor starts with ? and ends with &.
The query holds key-value pairs, first after ? then separated by &.
w: True: A name or an IP.
False: That is the query; the anchor starts with #.

6.q: A student sets the web root of a server to their home folder. Which statements are justified?
o: Private files such as keys and configs could be exposed.
On a LAN, everyone on the LAN could access the files.
It is safe because only the owner knows the port.
A dedicated folder with no confidential files is a better web root.
Testing on localhost first exposes no unfinished work.
w: True: Anyone who can reach the port can request them.
True: The server listens to the network.
False: Port scanning finds open ports.
True: Serve only what is meant to be public.
True: Loopback stays on the device.

6.q: Which statements about httpie and browsers are correct?
o: httpie shows the source HTML.
A browser shows the rendered page.
http --print b shows the body only.
http --print H shows the body only.
Right-click View Source shows the raw HTML in a browser.
w: True: After applying CSS and running scripts.
True: The option prints the response body.

6.q: Server on port 8000 is running. Which statements about nmap and the browser are correct?
o: nmap localhost -p 8000 shows open.
After Ctrl-C stops the server, nmap shows closed.
After the server stops, the browser cannot connect.
nmap shows filtered while the server runs on localhost.
A second server needs a different port, such as 9000.
6.e: Open while running, closed after stopping.
w: False: Filtered needs a firewall in the way.

6.q: Which statements about the web server and the web root are correct?
o: A web server binds a port and serves files from the web root.
A URL path is mapped to a file path under the web root.
Two servers on 8000 and 9000 can show different content.
The URL scheme names the folder to serve.
localhost:8000 and localhost:8888 reach the same server.
6.e: Port, root and path decide what you see.
w: True: Apache, Nginx and Python http.server do this.
True: The path is relative to the root.
False: The scheme is http or https.
False: Different ports reach different processes.

7.q: Which statements about a home LAN are correct?
o: The ONT converts optical signals from the ISP into electrical signals.
A consumer router is often a router, switch and Wi-Fi access point in one.
The switch and access point handle only local traffic.
The router has only a private IP.
The router is the default gateway.
w: True: Internet access is the router's job.
False: It also has a public one.
True: The exit to the Internet.

7.e: Check the boundaries of the 172 range.
w: False: Just above the private block, so public.
False: Just below the private block, so public.

7.q: Which statements about public and private IP addresses are correct?
o: A public IP is globally unique.
A private IP can be reused in different LANs.
A private IP is routable on the Internet.
Public IPs are allocated from ICANN through registries to ISPs.
A home router's public IP may change unless a static IP is bought.
7.e: Public is unique and routable; private is local.
w: True: No two Internet endpoints share one.
True: Such as APNIC for Asia-Pacific.

7.q: Which statements about DHCP are correct?
o: A device that joins the LAN asks for an address.
The router leases a private IP automatically.
DHCP translates private addresses into public ones.
The router can also lease other settings such as the default gateway.
DHCP only works with IPv6.
w: False: It is used on IPv4 LANs.

7.q: A laptop at 192.168.0.12 requests a web page. Which statements about NAT are correct?
o: The router replaces the private source address and port with its public address and a port.
The router records the mapping in a table.
The reply goes to the laptop's private IP directly across the Internet.
The router looks up the table and sends the reply to the laptop.
All devices behind the router appear to websites with the same public IP.
w: False: Private IPs are not routable.

7.q: Which statements about why NAT exists are correct?
o: IPv4 addresses are limited.
Giving every device a public IPv4 address is impractical and costly.
NAT is less critical with IPv6.
NAT is a replacement for a firewall.
NAT lets many private devices share one public address.
w: True: The address space is vast.
False: Hiding structure is a side effect, not a security control.

7.q: Two different home routers each give a laptop the address 192.168.0.12. Which statements are correct?
o: This is fine.
The two laptops conflict on the Internet.
Their public IPs will differ.
Within each LAN the address must be unique.
DHCP guarantees global uniqueness.
w: False: Private IPs are not visible there.
True: Each router has its own public address.
True: Two devices cannot share one.
False: It guarantees LAN uniqueness only.

7.q: A phone is on mobile data and then on home Wi-Fi. Which statements are generally justified?
o: On Wi-Fi its IP is usually private.
On mobile data its IP is usually public.
Its IP is always the same in both cases.
A website sees the router's public IP for a Wi-Fi connection.
Private IPs are used on the Internet backbone.
7.e: What a website sees may differ from the device's own address.
w: True: Assigned by the home router.
True: Unless a VPN or carrier NAT applies.
False: It changes with the network.

7.q: A web server on laptop W (1.2.3.4) listens on 8888. Which steps are in a sensible order for another computer X to reach it?
o: On W, nmap port 8888 shows closed before the server starts.
On W, start the web server on 8888.
On W, nmap 8888 shows open after starting.
On X, nmap 1.2.3.4 -p 8888 shows open, then browse http://1.2.3.4:8888.
On X, browse to http://localhost:8888.
w: True: Confirms the server uses the port.

7.q: Which are good practices for a LAN web server exercise?
o: Choose a web root with no confidential files.
Never expose sensitive data via local web servers.
Use strong Wi-Fi pre-shared keys.
Expect firewalls to allow ICMP always.
Clean up temporary web content afterwards.
w: True: Everyone on the LAN can read it.
False: Firewalls may block ping; that is normal.

8.q: Which statements about cloud computing are correct?
o: Resources are provided by a third party and managed over the Internet.
On-premise means the organisation owns and manages its own servers.
In the cloud you pay for the hardware whether or not you use it.
Gmail is an example of a cloud service.
The big three providers are AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
w: True: Capital cost, power, cooling and maintenance.
True: Provided over the Internet by Google.

8.q: Which statements about cloud deployment models are correct?
o: A public cloud is open to any subscriber.
A private cloud is for one organisation.
A community cloud is shared by organisations with similar needs.
A hybrid cloud combines other models.
The model depends on where the hardware is.
8.e: Who can use it, not where it sits.
w: True: For example private plus public.
False: It depends on who can use it.

8.q: Which statements about EC2 are correct?
o: It rents virtual computers; you choose CPU, memory, storage and OS.
You pay only while the instance runs.
Terminating an instance stops billing.
An AMI is the template used to start instances.
EC2 is the AWS storage service.
8.e: Compute that you launch and terminate.
w: False: S3 is storage; EC2 is compute.

8.q: Which statements about SSH are correct?
o: It provides encrypted remote access.
The private key stays on your computer.
The public key is placed on the instance.
The key proves who you are rather than encrypting each typed word separately.
If you delete the .pem you can simply download it again.
8.e: Lose the key and you lose the way in.
w: False: AWS does not keep it; you are permanently locked out.

8.q: Which statements about ssh -i is114-keypair.pem ec2-user@IP are correct?
o: -i names the private key file.
ec2-user is the login user on the instance.
IP is the public IP of the instance.
The key file permissions should be chmod u=rw,go=.
The command works with the key readable by everyone.

8.q: A Python HTTP server runs on port 80 of an EC2 instance, but nobody can browse to it. nmap says filtered. Which statements are justified?
o: The security group may lack an inbound rule for port 80.
The server may be running perfectly.
The server must have crashed.
Adding an inbound rule for 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 should fix it.
Browsers hang or time out.
w: True: Filtered hides the real state.
False: Closed would suggest that; filtered does not.
True: Dropped packets give no answer.

8.q: Which security group settings follow the typical hardening?
o: Allow 80 and 443 from 0.0.0.0/0.
Allow 22 only from administrator IP addresses.
Allow 22 from 0.0.0.0/0.
A security group is a firewall at the instance level.
0.0.0.0/0 means a single IP address.
w: False: SSH open to the whole Internet.
False: It means all IPv4 addresses.

o: Forgetting to terminate an instance means continuing charges.
Deleting the .pem causes permanent lock-out.
A .pem with open permissions is refused by ssh.
Terminating an instance keeps all data for free.
A running server with a missing port rule looks like an outage.
8.e: Small mistakes cost money or access.
w: True: Billing runs while it exists.

8.q: Which statements about AWS services and market are correct?
o: EC2 is compute.
S3 is storage.
RDS is a relational database service.
AWS is the market leader.
Azure is the market leader.
w: True: Roughly 30% share in the slides.

8.q: A company keeps sensitive financial data on private clusters and serves a public web app from AWS. This is best described as ...
o: a hybrid cloud.
a community cloud.
an on-premise only model.
it uses both private and public resources.
a single-tenant model throughout.
w: True: A combination of private and public.
False: That is shared between similar organisations.
False: Part runs on the public cloud.
True: That is the point of hybrid.

9.q: Which statements about the CIA triad are correct?
o: Confidentiality is protection from unauthorised access.
Integrity is modification only by appropriate mechanisms.
Availability is authorised access when needed.
Encryption alone guarantees integrity.
A DoS flood is an attack on availability.

9.q: Match scenarios to pillars. Which are correct?
o: A web root pointing at private files breaks confidentiality.
A tampered account balance breaks integrity.
Corrupted data from a transmission error breaks integrity.
A DoS flood breaks confidentiality.
An unreachable server breaks availability.
w: True: Authorised users cannot use it.

9.q: Which statements about authentication are correct?
o: Something you know includes a password or PIN.
Something you have includes a smart card or token.
Something you are is a biometric trait such as a fingerprint.
Two-factor authentication needs two forms of identification.
SMS one-time codes are the strongest factor.
w: True: For example a password and a device.

9.q: Which statements about passwords and password managers are correct?
o: A password should be easy to remember and hard to guess.
A password manager stores and autofills logins.
It encrypts its data and is protected by a master password.
You should enable extra protection such as 2FA.
Passwords are immune to phishing.
w: False: They can be tricked out of you.

9.q: Which statements about biometrics are correct?
o: A false rejection denies a legitimate user.
A false acceptance admits an impostor.
The system is tuned between the two.
A biometric scanner can never make mistakes.
A scanner rejecting a real user is a false rejection.
9.e: Tuning trades one error for the other.

9.q: Which statements about cryptography vocabulary are correct?
o: Plaintext is readable and ciphertext is not.
A cipher is the algorithm and the key guides it.
Cryptanalysis is decrypting without knowing the cipher or key.
A Caesar cipher is hard for modern computers to break.
Decrypt(FRPSXWHU) with shift 3 gives COMPUTER.
9.e: Substitution ciphers are weak; decryption shifts each letter back by the same amount.
w: False: Only 25 useful shifts exist, so it is easy to break.
True: Shift each letter back by 3.

9.q: Which statements about symmetric and public-key cryptography are correct?
o: Symmetric schemes use the same key to encrypt and decrypt.
Symmetric schemes have a key-distribution problem.
Public-key cryptography uses a public and a private key.
The public key encrypts and the private key decrypts.
The private key is sent along with the message.
9.e: The private key is never transmitted.
w: True: The secret must reach the receiver safely.

9.q: Which statements about firewalls are correct?
o: A firewall filters traffic according to an access control policy.
Port filtering can deny inbound port 22 from the Internet while allowing the LAN.
Stateful inspection tracks connection state.
Deep packet inspection is stronger but adds latency.
A firewall encrypts all traffic automatically.
9.e: Filter first; inspect more for more protection.

9.q: Which scenarios map correctly to a security concept?
o: HTTPS instead of HTTP → confidentiality and integrity.
chmod u=rw,go= key.pem → confidentiality of the private key.
A security group closing port 22 to the world → an access control policy.
A DoS flood on a server → confidentiality.
A biometric scanner rejecting a real user → false rejection.

9.q: Which statements about risk analysis and privileges are correct?
o: Risk analysis weighs the nature and likelihood of risks.
Its goal is to minimise vulnerability to the biggest threats.
Separation of management privileges splits administrative powers.
It means one administrator holds every power.
It pairs realistic threats with vulnerabilities.
9.e: Many hands, no single point of failure.
w: True: So no one person can compromise the system.

10.q: Which tiers and concepts are matched correctly?
o: Tier 1: sensors and wearables, embedded systems, Bluetooth.
Tier 2: ONT and router, DHCP and NAT.
Tier 3: AWS EC2, public cloud virtualisation.
Tier 4: Python web server and ML engine.
Tier 5: HTTP/HTTPS, HTML5/CSS, loopback testing.
10.e: Each tier has its own vocabulary.

10.q: Which statements about the data path are correct?
o: Sensors reach the home router.
Traffic leaves via the ONT and the ISP over HTTPS on 443.
The AWS security group filters the traffic before EC2.
Traffic goes straight to the clinical servers from the sensors.
The EC2 instance runs the application and the analytics.
w: False: It passes through the cloud instance.
True: Python web server and ML engine.

10.q: Which statements about the developer laptops are justified?
o: 16-32 GB RAM supports many concurrent processes.
A fast SSD shortens loading and build times.
Linux gives native sensor SDK support and CLI pipelines.
Linux is chosen because it cannot run virtual machines.
A multi-core CPU helps run several processes at once.
10.e: Hardware and OS choices serve the workflow.
w: False: Windows apps can run in VMs on Linux.

10.q: Which statements about the office network are correct?
o: The ISP terminates fibre in an ONT.
The router has one public IPv4 address on its WAN side.
DHCP leases Class C private addresses to laptops.
Each laptop needs its own public IP.
An internal DNS daemon maps internal hostnames to private IPs.
10.e: One public IP, many private IPs.
w: True: Then Ethernet to the router.

10.q: Why is the application first tested on loopback?
o: 127.0.0.1 never leaves the device.
It works without Internet access.
It exposes unfinished code to the public.
localhost:8000 and 127.0.0.1:8000 reach the same local server.
Rendering can be checked before provisioning cloud servers.

10.q: Which statements about the perimeter security are correct?
o: 80/443 are open to 0.0.0.0/0 so clients and sensors can connect.
22 is restricted to administrator IPs.
Developers authenticate with RSA keypairs.
The private key is protected with chmod u=rw,go=.
The private key is stored in authorized_keys.
10.e: Open what must be public; lock down the rest.
w: True: Public key on the instance.
False: The public key goes there.

10.q: Which statements about telemetry and alerts are correct?
o: Sensors send encrypted telemetry over HTTPS (443).
Prolonged inactivity can trigger automated alerts to caregivers.
Wearables send vitals to clinical servers.
HTTP on port 80 would also be encrypted.
The home router NATs the sensor traffic.
Port 443 appears in the application (HTTPS) and the security group.
Port 22 appears in the perimeter tier for SSH.
A private IP appears at tiers 1 and 2.
A public IP appears at tier 3.
A private IP appears on the EC2 instance as its Internet address.
10.e: Trace the concept through each tier.
w: False: Its Internet address is public.

10.q: Why use an EC2 instance rather than buying server hardware?
o: It can be provisioned in minutes.
You pay as you go.
No physical server needs to be bought and maintained.
It makes an SSH key unnecessary.
You can terminate it when no longer needed.

10.q: A Security Group lacks a rule for port 443, yet the web server runs on 443. Which statements are correct?
o: Sensors cannot deliver telemetry over HTTPS.
nmap from the Internet reports 443 as filtered.
The instance has crashed.
Adding an inbound rule for 443 fixes the symptom.
Alerts to caregivers might be delayed or lost.
10.e: Reachable only if a rule allows it.
w: True: Data cannot reach the application.

lessons.title: Computer Hardware
lessons.goal: Read a laptop specification and explain what the processor, RAM, storage, GPU and ports each do.
lessons.subtitle: Read a laptop specification and explain what the processor, RAM, storage, GPU and ports each do.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersEvery later topic, from processes to the cloud, runs on these parts. Knowing which part does what lets you explain why a computer is slow or why work is lost.
🧠 Memory hookCPU computes, RAM holds what is running, storage keeps what is saved. RAM forgets at power-off; storage does not.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1Hardware vs software→2Reading a laptop specification line by line→3Metric prefixes — powers of ten→4The processor (CPU)→5Memory (RAM) vs storage — the central compar…→6How it all works together (when you open a b…→7GPU, display, ports, wireless→8Embedded systems and the micro:bit→9Hardware gotchas
⚡ At a glance — the machine
Storage (non-volatile)→RAM (volatile)→Cache→CPU cores→Display, ports
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
RAMVolatile main memory that holds the programs and data in use now.Fast and empties at power-off; not the same as storage.
Storage (SSD/HDD)Non-volatile secondary memory for the OS, apps and files.Keeps data without power; slower than RAM.
CacheVery fast volatile memory on or near the CPU.Checked first, before RAM and storage.
CoreOne independent processor inside a multi-core CPU.More cores help parallel work and use more power.
GHzClock speed in billions of cycles per second.A speed unit, not a size unit.
🗺️ The whole course in one picture

IS114 walks bottom-up from the machine to the Internet and security: hardware → operating system → files & permissions → networks → the Web → LANs/NAT → cloud → security. Each layer relies on the one before it: a process (Chapter 2) needs RAM (Chapter 1); a web server (Chapter 6) is a process (Chapter 2) that listens on a port (Chapter 5) and serves files from a directory (Chapter 4); a cloud VM (Chapter 8) is just a remote Linux machine you reach by SSH using a protected key file (Chapters 4 and 9).

Concept map of the whole course. Read it clockwise from Chapter 1; each branch is a Part of these notes.

flowchart TD
  A[Storage SSD/HDD<br/>non-volatile] -->|program loaded into| B[RAM<br/>volatile]
  B -->|instructions and data| C[Cache]
  C --> D[CPU cores<br/>fetch decode execute]
  D --> E[GPU graphics]
  D -->|results| B
  B -->|save| A
  D --> F[Display and ports]

How storage, RAM, cache and CPU cooperate when you open a program (cache position inferred from). Note the CPU never executes straight from storage — programs are copied into RAM first.

1.1Hardware vs software
TermMeaning
HardwarePhysical parts you can touch; "visible even when powered off", consuming no electricity. Examples: processor, memory, storage, battery, keyboard, screen, ports.
SoftwarePrograms and data that run on hardware (OS, web browser, word processor).

A computing system = hardware + software. In the Week 1 specification, the single software item is Windows 11 Home.

1.2Reading a laptop specification line by line

The course reference specification:

Spec lineMeaning
Intel Core i7CPU model — a high-performance processor.
2.8 GHzClock speed = 2.8 billion cycles per second.
Quad-Core4 cores for parallel processing / better multitasking.
12 MB Intel Smart CacheVery fast volatile memory inside the CPU; 12 MB = 12 million bytes.
15-inch HD LED display (1920 × 1080)15 inches = diagonal screen size; HD = High Definition; LED = Light-Emitting Diode backlight (energy-efficient, long-lasting, mercury-free); 1920 × 1080 = resolution in pixels, width × height.
Intel Iris Xe GPUGraphics Processing Unit: handles graphics (games, video, animation); relieves the CPU.
20 GB RAMRandom Access Memory (main memory); 20 GB = 20 billion bytes; volatile.
1 TB SSDSolid-State Drive (secondary storage); 1 TB = 1 trillion bytes; non-volatile; faster and more durable than HDD (no moving parts).
WiFi 7, Bluetooth 5WiFi: wireless internet (long range). Bluetooth: short-range wireless for keyboards, earphones, phone syncing.
2 USB Type-C portsUniversal Serial Bus: connects external devices (flash drives, monitors, phones).
1 HDMI portHigh-Definition Multimedia Interface: sends video and audio to TVs/projectors.
3 kgWeight.
Windows 11 HomePre-installed operating system (software).
1.3Metric prefixes — powers of ten
PrefixSymbolValueIn bytes
Kilo-K10³1,000 B
Mega-M10⁶1,000,000 B
Giga-G10⁹1,000,000,000 B
Tera-T10¹²1,000,000,000,000 B
Peta-P10¹⁵1 quadrillion B

(in words: kilo = thousand, mega = million, giga = billion, tera = trillion, peta = quadrillion)

Course rule: use powers of 10 (1 KB = 1,000 B). Ignore binary prefixes (KiB, MiB, GiB). shows the prefixes up to Tera; Peta appears in and.

Worked example. The spec lists 20 GB RAM. 20 GB = 20 × 10⁹ = 20,000,000,000 bytes. If one ASCII character is 1 byte, RAM could in principle hold 20 billion characters (ignoring OS overhead). Emoji are usually 4 bytes each, so the same RAM holds roughly 5×10⁹ emoji.

1.4The processor (CPU)

Synonyms: CPU, Central Processing Unit, microprocessor, microcontroller. Think of it as "the brain".

PartWhat it isWhy it matters
FunctionFetch instructions and data from memory, decode, execute; process data (text, images, numbers)The only component that actually computes.
ClockA centrally generated series of electrical pulses that coordinates all actions in the computer. Measured in Hz (cycles per second); 2.8 GHz = 2.8 billion cycles/second.The "conductor's baton" . Higher GHz → more cycles per second.
CoresA multi-core CPU has several independent processors in one chip (Dual/Quad/Hexa).More cores = better performance and higher power usage (and more heat and cost).
CacheVery fast volatile memory on/near the CPU storing frequently used data/instructions (typically 8–12 MB).Avoids waiting on slower RAM.

Lookup order when the CPU needs data: cache (fastest) → RAM → storage (slowest, last resort). The CPU tries the fastest place first to avoid delays. Note states this "is not stated explicitly in the notes, and requires inference".

1.5Memory (RAM) vs storage — the central comparison
AttributeMemory (RAM)Storage (SSD/HDD)
SynonymsRAM, primary storage/memory, main memory, volatile memorySecondary storage, disk, non-volatile memory
VolatilityVolatile — all contents lost when power is offNon-volatile — retained without power
RoleHolds the OS, programs and data currently in useLong-term storage of OS, apps, files
CPU accessCPU reads from and writes to it directly; programs execute from hereCPU cannot execute from storage; program must be loaded into RAM first
Typical capacity4–32 GB in laptops/phones;: 4 GB basic, 16 GB standard, 32 GB high-end200 GB–1 TB;: 256 GB–1 TB laptops, several TB desktops/servers; summary table 256 GB–2 TB
SpeedFast (but slower than cache)Slower ("storage is slower than RAM but permanent")
Effect of too littleOS closes programs to free space; too many apps feel sluggishLess room for files and apps

Storage types: SSD — no moving parts, fast, durable, expensive; HDD — spinning disk, slower, cheaper, more fragile; SD card — removable (cameras, phones).

Hardware summary table:

ComponentCategoryVolatile?SpeedTypical sizeRole
CPUProcessorn/aFastestn/aExecutes instructions
CacheMemoryYesVery fast8–12 MBSpeeds up CPU access
RAMMemoryYesFast4–32 GBRun programs & store active data
SSD/HDDStorageNoSlower256 GB–2 TBStore OS, apps, files long-term
GPUProcessorn/aFastIntegrated or dedicatedHandle graphics

Unsaved work. Because RAM is volatile, anything you are editing that hasn't been saved to storage is lost immediately on sudden power loss. A running process dies on power-off, while its program file survives on storage (see §2.5).

🧩 Pause & recall — Why must a program be copied into RAM before it runs?
Answer: The CPU reads and executes instructions from RAM, not directly from storage. Storage is the permanent copy; RAM is the working copy.
1.6How it all works together (when you open a browser)
  1. Storage loads the program into RAM.
  2. RAM supplies data/instructions to the CPU.
  3. CPU executes instructions and processes data.
  4. GPU handles graphics (video, animations).
  5. Results are shown on screen and saved back to storage if needed.

"This cycle runs millions of times per second." The von Neumann architecture: instructions (software) and data are both stored in the memory unit.

1.7GPU, display, ports, wireless
  • GPU: a separate processor for graphics; frees the CPU; also used for machine-learning tasks and parallel matrix computations.
  • Display: size = diagonal of the screen; resolution = pixels wide × high (1920 × 1080 → 1,920 pixels across, 1,080 down).
  • USB: standardised bidirectional interface for data and power. HDMI: uncompressed digital audio + video to monitors/TVs.
  • Bluetooth: short range, low power → ideal for keyboards, mice, earphones.
1.8Embedded systems and the micro:bit

An embedded system is a computer dedicated to a narrow range of functions as part of a larger system — found in microwaves, cars, watches, medical equipment, smart appliances.

The BBC micro:bit v2 is a tiny embedded computer with a processor, memory, storage and sensors; in the lab it is "a platform to practice coding and sensor integration". It demonstrates that the same three resources (processor, memory, storage) exist even in a tiny device.

1.9Hardware gotchas
  • Memory ≠ storage. A big disk does not let you run more programs at once; RAM does. (A machine with lots of storage but little RAM still feels slow when many apps run.)
  • Storage is not "executed" directly. The CPU runs programs from RAM.
  • Prefix confusion: 1 TB = 10¹² bytes in this course, not 2⁴⁰.
  • Quad-Core ≠ 4× faster in every case; it helps parallel work, and costs power.
  • 15-inch is the diagonal, not width.
⚡ Quick examples
Volatile or not?
PointRAM loses its contents at power-off; storage keeps them.
ExampleAn unsaved document is lost in a power cut, but the saved file survives.
ExplanationOnly storage is non-volatile, so only saved work persists.
Decimal prefixes
PointThe course uses powers of ten: 1 GB = 10⁹ bytes.
Example20 GB of RAM is 20,000,000,000 bytes.
ExplanationIgnore the binary prefixes (KiB, MiB, GiB) in this course.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • CPU = fetch, decode, execute; clock speed is in GHz; more cores help parallel work.
  • Lookup order for data: cache, then RAM, then storage.
  • RAM is volatile and holds what is running; storage is non-volatile and holds what is saved.
  • Programs are copied from storage into RAM before the CPU runs them.
  • 1 KB = 1,000 B, 1 MB = 10⁶ B, 1 GB = 10⁹ B, 1 TB = 10¹² B.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Hardwaretap to flip
The physical parts of a computer that you can touch, such as the processor, memory, storage and ports.
Softwaretap to flip
Programs and data that run on the hardware, including the operating system and applications.
CPU (processor)tap to flip
Fetches, decodes and executes instructions and processes data; the only part that actually computes.
Clock speed (GHz)tap to flip
Cycles per second. 2.8 GHz is 2.8 billion cycles per second.
Coretap to flip
An independent processor inside a multi-core CPU. More cores help parallel work but cost more power.
Cachetap to flip
Very fast volatile memory on or near the CPU that holds frequently used data. Checked before RAM.
➡ Where next? Hardware does nothing alone. Next, the operating system decides which program gets the CPU, RAM and storage.

lessons.title: Operating Systems & Processes
lessons.goal: Explain what an operating system does, why Linux and the command line matter, and how processes differ from programs.
lessons.subtitle: Explain what an operating system does, why Linux and the command line matter, and how processes differ from programs.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersEvery program you run goes through the OS. Understanding processes and the shell is what lets you control a computer instead of only clicking it.
🧠 Memory hookSharing nicely. The OS shares the CPU, RAM and storage among every program that wants them.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1Software categories→2Roles of an OS — "sharing nicely"→3Why Linux?→4GUI vs CLI→5Program vs process→6Process control commands
⚡ At a glance — the OS sits in the middle
User or app→GUI / CLI→Operating system→CPU · RAM · storage
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Application softwarePrograms written to solve a user need.Firefox, Office, games.
System softwareSoftware that manages the computer at a basic level.Windows, Linux, macOS.
ProgramAn executable file stored on disk.Sits in storage and survives power-off.
ProcessA program in execution.Lives in RAM and ends at power-off.
Foreground / backgroundForeground is what you interact with; background runs without interaction.Ctrl-z suspends; bg and fg resume.
2.1Software categories
CategoryDefinitionExamples
Application softwareWritten to address specific needs / solve real-world problemsTerminal, Microsoft Office, Firefox, Chrome, games, social media, AI tools
System softwareManages a computer system at a fundamental level; provides tools for creating and running application software, often interacts directly with hardwareWindows, Linux, macOS

The operating system (OS) is the core component of system software.

2.2Roles of an OS — "sharing nicely"

An OS:

  1. Manages computer resources such as memory and storage (and processors).
  2. Provides an interface through which a human can interact with the computer.
  3. Allows application programs to interact with those resources.

All roles revolve around "sharing nicely": resources are shared among programs that want them. The course notes break this into four duties:

DutyWhat it means
Processor schedulingPrograms take turns on the CPU so all make progress ()
Memory allocationIsolated RAM space per process; reclaimed on termination
Storage & I/O coordinationTurns file requests into low-level block reads/writes
User interfacesGUI and CLI

Booting: when the machine powers up, firmware loads the OS (kernel) from non-volatile storage into memory and hands control of the computer to it.

flowchart TD
  U[User] --> UI[User interface: GUI or CLI]
  UI --> OS[Operating system]
  APP[Application programs] --> OS
  OS --> CPU[Processor scheduling]
  OS --> MEM[Memory allocation]
  OS --> STO[Storage and I/O]
  CPU --> HW[Hardware]
  MEM --> HW
  STO --> HW

Caption: the OS sits between users/applications and hardware (figure re-expressed; box labels inferred). Notice every request, whether from a person or a program, passes through the OS.

2.3Why Linux?
  • Used in this course to prepare for advanced IS courses.
  • Powers over 60% of servers worldwide and all of the Top 500 supercomputers.
  • Android is built on the open-source Linux kernel.
2.4GUI vs CLI
GUICLI
InteractionClick or tap graphical elementsType commands
StrengthIntuitive for single itemsBatch processing, automation (scripting), remote administration with little bandwidth
Other names—terminal, shell, command line

Why beginners struggle with the Linux CLI: it is case-sensitive and needs precise syntax; also forgetting to check the prompt host, not using tab-completion, and confusing signals.

CLI conventions: commands are almost always lowercase; options typically come before arguments; the order of options does not matter. Tricks: Tab completion; history with ↑ / ↓; Ctrl+c stops a running command.

Which computer am I on? Look at the prompt: it shows the username and the hostname of the machine you're commanding.

2.5Program vs process
ProgramProcess
DefinitionAn executable file with a set of instructions (and data)A program in execution
Lives inStorage (non-volatile) — e.g. /bin/cat, C:\Windows\notepad.exeMain memory (RAM)
When power is cutRemains intactTerminates instantly (RAM is volatile)

Synonyms for program: app, application, executable file.

See them: Programs — Windows Start ➜ Settings ➜ Apps; macOS Finder ➜ Applications. Processes — Windows Task Manager; macOS Activity Monitor. Try opening and closing Notepad/Calculator and watch the process appear and vanish.

Foreground vs background: the foreground process is the one you're interacting with right now; background processes run without direct user interaction. GUI analogies: foreground ≈ maximised app you are using; background ≈ minimised/behind other windows; Ctrl-C ≈ closing the app.

2.6Process control commands
CommandPurpose
ps uList processes you own (note: no dash — ps -u is ❌ in this course)
topInteractive demo process (used to practise control)
Ctrl-cTerminate (kill) the foreground process
Ctrl-zSuspend (pause) the foreground process
bgResume the most recently suspended process in the background
fgResume the most recently suspended process in the foreground

Focus on the COMMAND column of ps u — it shows the program, options and arguments.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Foreground: start command
  Foreground --> Suspended: Ctrl-z
  Suspended --> Foreground: fg
  Suspended --> Background: bg
  Background --> Foreground: fg
  Foreground --> [*]: Ctrl-c (killed)
  Background --> [*]: finishes or killed

Caption: process state control in Linux (the Background → Foreground and finish edges are inferred). A killed process frees both CPU and RAM; a suspended process uses zero CPU but still holds its RAM until resumed or killed.

Worked trace — "I pressed Ctrl-Z by mistake":

  1. You meant to kill top, but pressed Ctrl-Z. top is paused and moved out of the foreground.
  2. Type fg → it returns to the foreground.
  3. Press Ctrl-c → it is terminated.

Common beginner mistake: pressing Ctrl-Z by accident and wondering where the process went — it's paused, not gone. "Suspending vs sleeping" are different concepts, out of scope.

🧩 Pause & recall — You press Ctrl-z by mistake while running top. Is it gone?
Answer: No. It is suspended, not killed. Type fg to bring it back, then Ctrl-c to terminate it.
⚡ Quick examples
Process control
PointCtrl-c kills the foreground process; Ctrl-z suspends it.
ExampleCtrl-z, then bg, runs it in the background; fg brings it back.
ExplanationA suspended process uses no CPU but still holds its RAM.
Program vs process
PointA program is a file; a process is that program running.
Examplenotepad.exe on disk is a program; the open Notepad window is a process.
ExplanationCut the power and the process dies while the file remains.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • The OS manages resources, provides a user interface and lets applications use resources.
  • Four duties: scheduling the CPU, allocating memory, coordinating storage and I/O, and user interfaces.
  • A program is an executable file in storage; a process is a program in execution in RAM.
  • Ctrl-c kills, Ctrl-z suspends, bg resumes in the background, fg resumes in the foreground.
  • Use ps u (no dash) to list your processes.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Application softwaretap to flip
Software written to address specific user needs, such as a browser, office suite or game.
System softwaretap to flip
Software that manages the computer at a fundamental level and runs applications. Windows, Linux and macOS are examples.
Operating system (OS)tap to flip
The core of system software. It manages resources, provides a user interface and lets applications use resources. All of this is "sharing nicely".
Processor schedulingtap to flip
Programs take turns on the CPU so that all make progress.
Memory allocationtap to flip
Each process gets an isolated space in RAM, which is reclaimed when it ends.
Bootingtap to flip
On power-up, firmware loads the OS (kernel) from non-volatile storage into memory and hands control to it.

lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersReal data arrives as text files. A short pipeline answers questions in seconds that would take minutes in a spreadsheet.
🧠 Memory hookSkip the header, cut the column, sort, then uniq. uniq only removes neighbours, so sort always comes first.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1File-system listing and file commands→2Extract, search, sort, count→3Lab 1 dataset — yum.csv→4Lab 1 — all 28 tasks with answers→5Pipeline explanations→6Redirection traces
⚡ At a glance — a counting pipeline
tail -n +2→cut -d, -f2→sort→uniq -c→sort -n -r→head
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
cut -d -fExtracts fields (columns); -d sets the delimiter, -f the field numbers.Takes columns; grep takes rows.
grepPrints the lines that match a pattern; -i ignores case, -v inverts.Case-sensitive by default.

3.1File-system listing and file commands
CommandPurpose

3.2Extract, search, sort, count

grep "text" filePrint lines matching-i ignore case, -v invert (lines not matching)

|Pipe: output of one command → input of the next
* ?Wildcards: * = any characters (zero or more); ? = exactly one character

Wildcard examples: ls *.csv, ls so*, ls s?m?.

Which commands accept multiple files?

Accepts several filesDoes not
cat *.csv, ls f1 f2, wc *.log, head f1 f2, tail f1 f2, sort f1 f2, grep "error" *.logcut → use cat files | cut …; uniq → use cat files | sort | uniq

Pipes: cat file | grep "dog" | sort | uniq -c; cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | sort | uniq -c.

Redirection: > creates/overwrites; >> appends. Overwrite also truncates: > file.txt empties a file but keeps it.

🧩 Pause & recall — Why does sort come before uniq in a pipeline?
Answer: uniq only removes adjacent duplicates. sort puts equal lines next to each other first.

(Within a Markdown table the pipe is escaped as \|; type a plain | in the terminal.)

Worked trace — task 27 (input → output at each stage, added context computed from the dataset):

  1. tail -n +2 yum.csv → 20 data rows (header dropped; +2 means "start from line 2").
  2. cut -d',' -f2 → 20 food names.
  3. sort → alphabetical, so identical names are adjacent (Green Milk Tea, Green Milk Tea, … Sushi, Sushi, Sushi).
  4. uniq -c → counts, e.g. 3 Sushi, 2 Nasi Lemak, 2 Green Milk Tea, others 1.
  5. sort -n -r → numeric descending: 3 Sushi first, then the 2s.
  6. head -n 2 → top 2 lines. (Ties at count 2 are ordered by the secondary text of the line, so which 2 appears second is decided by the sort's tie-break — added context.)

Worked trace — task 3 vs 21: grep "Sushi" yum.csv | wc -l counts lines containing "Sushi" = 3 (2020-01-11, two on 2020-01-19). It counts lines, not occurrences within a line.

Why grep ",5," in task 28? It matches the price column exactly (,5,) and avoids prices like 15 or 50.

Best practices: always skip the header with tail -n +2 yum.csv (more reliable than grep -v "#"); use ',' as the cut delimiter for CSV; sort -n -r for descending top-N; uniq -c only after sort; chain with pipes.

Key rules recap: ps u, not ps -u · quotes for spaces, not \ · grep is case-sensitive by default · *always sort before uniq** · uniq only works on adjacent lines · cut -d',' for CSV · `= any chars,?= one char · don't usewc -c`.

3.5Pipeline explanations
  • cat yum.csv | grep "Sushi" | wc -l — stream file, keep lines containing "Sushi", count them.
  • cat yum.csv | grep -v "#date" | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c — drop the header row, extract column 2 (food), sort, count each unique food.

powershell

powershell

⚡ Quick examples
Skip the header
Pointtail -n +2 starts output from line 2.
Exampletail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d"," -f2
ExplanationThe header row would otherwise be counted and sorted as data.
> versus >>

Exampleecho "a" > f; echo "b" > f leaves one line, b.
ExplanationOverwriting also truncates: > file empties it but keeps the file.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • cut takes columns (-d delimiter, -f field); grep takes rows; sort orders lines; uniq collapses neighbours; wc -l counts lines.
  • Always sort before uniq, and use sort -n for numbers.
  • tail -n +2 skips a header row.
  • Pipe (|) feeds one command into the next; > overwrites and >> appends.
  • * matches any characters, ? matches exactly one.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
ls, ls -l, ls -atap to flip

Sorts lines. -r reverses; -n sorts numerically; the default is alphabetical.

Removes adjacent duplicate lines. -c counts, -d shows duplicates, -u shows unique lines. Sort first.

lessons.title: File Systems, Paths & Permissions
lessons.goal: Navigate a directory tree with absolute and relative paths and control access with chmod.
lessons.subtitle: Navigate a directory tree with absolute and relative paths and control access with chmod.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it mattersEvery command works on files. Reading paths correctly and setting permissions is how you avoid deleting the wrong thing or exposing a private key.
🧠 Memory hookAbsolute starts with /, relative starts from here. chmod: who (u g o a), operator (+ - =), then r w x.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1Core definitions→2Text files vs binary files→3File types and extensions→4File operations→5Directory trees and paths→6The PATH environment variable→7Navigation and manipulation commands→8File protection and permissions→9Lab 2 — walking the is114-nav tree (27 steps)→10Filesystem gotchas
⚡ At a glance — read a path, then a permission
Root /→Directory tree→Absolute or relative→chmod u=rw,go=
🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Absolute pathA path from the root; always starts with /.Starts with /, unique anywhere.
Relative pathA path from the current working directory.Never starts with /.
CWD (pwd)The directory you are in now.pwd prints it.
. and ... is the current directory; .. is the parent.cd . stays; cd .. goes up.
r / w / xRead, write, execute.On a directory, x means enter (cd).
4.1Core definitions
TermDefinition
FileA named collection of related data, used for organizing secondary memory; from the user's view, the smallest amount of data that can be written to storage
File systemThe operating system's logical view of the files it manages
DirectoryA named group of files (also "folder")

Why directories? They group and organise files logically, and a directory tree lets filenames be reused in different subdirectories.

Linux filenames are case-sensitive: data.txt and Data.txt are different files and can coexist. Mistyping a name can therefore act on the wrong file.

4.2Text files vs binary files
Text fileBinary file
ContentCharacters from a character set (ASCII, Unicode)Data in a specific format needing special interpretation of its bits (formatting, pixels, audio…)
Human-readable?Yes — open in a text editorNo — gibberish without proper software
Examples.txt .csv .java .html .sh.docx .jpg .mp3 .pdf .exe
Editable with nano?YesNo (or you corrupt it)

Misconception alert: "Text files aren't binary" is false. Everything on a computer is stored as binary digits; "text" vs "binary" is about how the bits are interpreted — text files are chunks of 8 or 16 bits interpreted as characters. The terms "are somewhat misleading".

A .docx is binary because it embeds formatting, fonts, margins, colours and media beside the text.

4.3File types and extensions
  • File type = the kind of information in a file. Extension = the part after the dot (.jpg, .csv) that indicates the type; names are Filename.Extension.
  • Purpose: helps the OS choose which program opens the file (MyProg.java → code editor; family.jpg → image viewer).
  • Extension ≠ truth. Renaming virus.exe to funny-cat.jpg does not change what it is. Changing an extension (or any part of the name) does not change the contents; you can't "convert" a file by renaming.
  • What happens on double-click: OS checks extension → opens associated program → program reads the real format → mismatch gives an error.
4.4File operations
OperationCommand / meaning
Createtouch (file), mkdir (folder)
Deleterm (file); rmdir (empty dir); rm -r (dir + contents)
Open / CloseLoad into a program (e.g. nano file.txt) / exit program
Rename / Movemv old new
Copycp source dest
Readcat, head, grep
Write>, nano
Append>>
Truncate> file.txt (delete content, keep file)
4.5Directory trees and paths
TermDefinition
Parent directoryThe containing directory
SubdirectoryThe directory being contained
Directory treeLogical view of nested directories
Root directoryHighest level: / (Linux), C:\ (Windows)
Current working directory (CWD)Where you are now (pwd)

Caption: a UNIX-style tree using examples /home/smith/reports/week1.txt and the two util.zip files (tree shape inferred from the paths). The two util.zip files coexist because their full paths differ.

Absolute path — begins at the root, always starts with /, unique and unambiguous. Examples: /, /bin/tar, /etc/sysconfig/clock, /home/smith/reports/week1.txt. Windows: C:\Program Files\MS Office\WinWord.exe.

Relative path — starts from the CWD, never starts with /. If CWD is /home/jones:

Relative pathResolves to

Special names: . = current directory; .. = parent directory. Find your absolute path with pwd.

4.6The PATH environment variable

PATH is a colon-separated list of directories searched for executables: PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/bin:/home/jones/utilities. The OS searches them in order and runs the first match. If printall is in a listed directory you can type printall from anywhere; otherwise type /home/jones/utilities/printall. Temporary addition: export PATH=$PATH:/home/jones/utilities (how to add is out of scope).

4.7Navigation and manipulation commands
CommandDescription
tree / tree FOLDERVisual tree from the current / specified folder
pwdPrint current working directory
cd / cd ~Go to home directory (same)
cd ..Up to parent
cd .Stay (no change)
cd -Previous working directory (toggle)
ls, ls -l, ls -aList; detailed; include hidden
mkdir DIR / rmdir DIRCreate / remove empty directory
rm FILE / rm -r DIRDelete file / directory recursively
mv OLD NEWMove or rename
cp F1 F2 / cp -r D1 D2Copy file / directory recursively
cat FILEDisplay
> FILE / >> FILEOverwrite / append

rm, mv, cp, > and >> "can permanently change or delete data. Use them carefully!" Deleting a directory deletes everything inside.

Hidden files: names starting with .. After mkdir one .two three, plain ls shows only one and three; use ls -a to see .two.

4.8File protection and permissions

File protection limits file access; in multi-user systems it is of primary importance. Three user categories and three permission bits:

CategorySymbolMeaning
OwneruThe user who owns the file (usually creator)
GroupgA set of users, e.g. project team
World/OtheroEveryone else with an account
(All)aall three
PermissionOn a fileOn a directory
r readView contents (cat, nano)List contents (ls)
w writeModify/overwrite/append/truncateCreate, delete, rename items inside
x executeRun as a program/scriptEnter / traverse (cd)

chmod

Syntax: chmod [who][operator][permissions] FILE, with who ∈ {u,g,o,a}, operator ∈ {+ add, - remove, = set exactly}, permissions ∈ {r,w,x}.

CommandEffect
chmod u+x script.shOwner can execute
chmod +x fileAll can execute (a+x)
chmod -x fileRemove execute from everyone
chmod go-w notes.txtRemove write from group and world
chmod u=rw,go=r fileOwner read/write; group/world read only
chmod u=rw,go= fileOnly owner read/write; nothing for group/world — private file (e.g. SSH key)
chmod u=rwx,go=rx dir/Owner full; others can enter and list but not create/delete
chmod u=r,go= FILEOwner read only, no write/execute; nothing for group/world

Note: chmod u=rw, go=r file in contains a stray space — the real syntax has no spaces around the comma.

Why must executable permission be granted explicitly? So you don't accidentally run a malicious downloaded file. A downloaded script run as ./this-is-running.sh gives Permission denied until chmod u+x this-is-running.sh.

Diagnosing permission symptoms (applications):

SymptomMissing permission
Can ls a folder ABC but cd ABC → Permission deniedx on the directory
Teammate can ls report.docx but cannot open itr on the file for their category — Group if in the file's group, otherwise World
Make a folder non-writable by everyone but the ownerchmod go-w FOLDER_NAME
World-readable, not writable fileAny user can view; cannot modify/delete
chmod u=rw,go= resultOnly owner can read/write
🧩 Pause & recall — You can ls a folder but cd into it says Permission denied. What is missing?
Answer: The execute (x) permission on the directory. r lets you list names; x lets you enter.
